sub: The safety margin in every bar.
points: Some oil is left unreacted so no lye is left over.

fb_text:
UK soap makers: what does "superfat" actually mean? 🧼

Superfat is the extra oil left in your soap on purpose, after all the lye has reacted.

✅ It's your safety margin, so no unreacted lye is left in the bar
✅ Around 5% is a common starting point for a gentle, long-lasting bar
✅ Push it very high and bars can feel greasy, go soft and spoil sooner
✅ Your lye calculator sets it for you, never guess it

fb_text:
Kiwi soap makers: which trace do you actually need? 🥄

Trace is the point where oils and caustic soda solution have emulsified and the batter starts to thicken.

✅ Light trace (thin custard): best for swirls and mixing colours
✅ Medium trace (pudding): holds a layer on top of another
✅ Thick trace (mashed potato): for textured tops and peaks

In a warm summer kitchen, trace comes faster, so have everything ready before you start blending.

sub: It's soda ash. Here's how to stop it.
points: Soda ash is cosmetic. The bar is fine to use.
Spritz fresh soap with 99% isopropyl alcohol, then cover.
Steam it off or plane the top.
fb_text:
White, chalky powder on top of your soap? 🤍

That's soda ash. It forms when unsaponified lye on the surface meets the air. It's harmless and only cosmetic.

✅ Spritz freshly poured soap with 99% isopropyl alcohol, then cover the mold
✅ Using a little less water in your recipe can help
✅ Already got it? Steam it off or plane the top for a clean finish

hook: Why is my soap still soft?
points: Extra water means slower to firm up.
High olive or sunflower needs more time.
UK damp slows curing. Air it well.
fb_text:
UK soap makers: bars still soft days after cutting? 🧼

✅ Too much water: more water means slower to firm up. Many makers use less than the old 38% default
✅ Lots of soft oils: high olive, sunflower or rice bran recipes need longer
✅ Damp air: a damp UK winter slows curing, so give bars airflow and a dry room

Soft doesn't mean ruined. Most bars harden with time.

sub: Why every change needs a recalculation.
points: Each needs its own amount of lye (SAP value).
Swapping can leave lye in the bar.
Change one oil, run the recipe again.
fb_text:
Out of olive oil, so you swap in sunflower? Stop and recalculate first ⚠️

Every oil needs a different amount of lye to turn into soap (its SAP value).

✅ Same weight of a different oil = a different amount of lye needed
✅ Skip the recalculation and you can end up with a harsh, lye-heavy bar or a soft, greasy one
✅ Change one oil, run the whole recipe through a lye calculator again
